body:
Fixes #99

## What changed
Adds `workday` and `weekend` properties to the `Job` class to allow scheduling tasks on weekdays (Monday-Friday) or weekends (Saturday-Sunday). title: fix: guard self.unit against None in Job.__repr__
body:
## Summary

Guard `self.unit` against `None` in `Job.__repr__()` to prevent a `TypeError` crash.

## Problem

When `self.unit` is `None` (its initial value at [line 233](https://github.com/dbader/schedule/blob/master/schedule/__init__.py#L233)) and `self.interval == 1`, calling `repr()` or `str()` on the Job crashes:

```python
>>> import schedule
>>> job = schedule.every(1)
>>> repr(job)
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable
```

This happens because `self.unit[:-1]` is called at lines 305 and 320 without first checking if `self.unit` is `None`.

## Fix

```diff
-  self.unit[:-1] if self.interval == 1 else self.unit,
+  self.unit[:-1] if self.unit and self.interval == 1 else self.unit,
```

Applied to both occurrences (lines 305 and 320).

Fixes #646

title: fix: guard against self.unit being None in Job.__repr__
body:
hit this on jobs that hadn't had a unit set yet:

    TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable

`self.unit` is initialized to `None` (there's even an `Optional[str]` type hint on it) but `__repr__` slices it unconditionally:

    self.unit[:-1] if self.interval == 1 else self.unit

so the moment you try to repr a freshly-constructed Job before the unit is set, it blows up. guarded both branches of the ternary with a `None` check and used "[unit not set]" as placeholder text.

fixes #646.

title: Improved timezones handling in next_run
body:
This improves how the timezone configured in `.at("18:00", "Europe/Amsterdam")` is processed.

The problem is that the `self.next_run value` is localized to `self.at_time_zone` and then converted to local time. In the next condition, the code uses `datetime.datetime.now()`, which fetches the current time in the local timezone. If the system's local timezone is different from `self.at_time_zone`, this can result in a discrepancy and cause the computation of self.next_run to be off by a day or more. This is what is happening in #603.

This PR changes the timezone-handling approach to use localized datetimes throughout the whole `_schedule_next_run` function.

PR created as draft since there are still a few untested cases that I would like to add tests for before merging. Especially in the area of combining `.at()` with weekdays, `until()` and daylight-saving-time.

title: Added parameter passthrough to run_pending for passing on output of scheduled method
body:
**Summary**

When calling _schedule.run_pending_ on either the _default_scheduler_ object in the module or a given instance of the class, it was desired for me to get the output data from the scheduled method, since in my application, _schedule.run_pending_ is constantly being polled in an async method loop.

Whenever the scheduled method was called I was unable to pipe the output from the method through to the front end without using shared state. 

To combat this, an optional parameter with default value as **False** was added called *passthrough* where it will in that case, add the method for the job in a dictionary as the key, and the returned value as the value behind this key while in the for-loop. It will then return the dictionary for the caller to unpack as desired.

This way, our discord bot can use scheduler as a way to call methods in nested object structures and return any output from them without having any shared state.

title: Support human readable expression
body:
In this PR, I add a `when` method to the Scheduler. With this function, we can store plain text schedule expression in text files, like what cron does with `/etc/crontab` file . A file using this idea may look like:

```
every day at 10:00, backup files
every day at 00:00, clean trash
every 60 minutes, go to toilet
```

title: Add timezone support for .at()
body:
Add a timezone parameter to the `.at()` method:
```python
schedule.every().day.at("12:42", "Asia/Jakarta").do(job)
```

During next-job-calculation, the next run is translated from the set timezone into the local timezone so that all jobs are being scheduled in the same timezone.

This implementation of timezone-support is inspired by #471, difference here is that [pytz](https://pypi.org/project/pytz/) is an optional dependency. Pytz is only required when using timezones. This ensures that people can keep using `schedule` without other dependencies.

What do you think? Feedback & Reviews is welcome!

title: Zero out accumulated time drift, and assert cron-like behaviour
body:
The time diff between when `run()` is called, and when `self.last_run`
is assigned accumulates as time drift. If left unchecked, `run()` is
triggered later and later from the ideal trigger point at the 'top' of
the unit of trigger time.

For example, if

```
schedule.every().minute.do(job)
```

is called at precisely 10:45:12, and the job takes 1 second to run,
before this commit the job execution start times would appear roughly
like:

```
10:45:12
10:46:13
10:47:14
10:48:15
```

But, `schedule` is meant to replicate cron's behaviour. This means that
for the same 'every minute' job, the job execution start time should
look like:

```
10:46:00
10:47:00
10:48:00
```

Solve both these problems by zeroing out next_run's units that are
accumulating drift - these are units smaller than the unit of trigger
time. This both accounts for time drift and asserts the cron-like
behaviour of triggering at the 'top' of the corresponding time.

title: Updated README Usage to work with function argument
body:
This PR is about a few changes on the README file, where I added demo usages because people mostly find and wanted to work with function arguments instantly. I created this PR because there are more lazy people like me who will find it useful.

Another example given below is to work with multiple arguments.

```python
import schedule
import time

def job():
    print("I'm working...")

""" working with multiple argument """
def function_job(name, age):
    print(f"I am {name} and my age is: {age}")

schedule.every(10).seconds.do(job)
schedule.every(10).seconds.do(function_job, name="Peter Griffin", age=22)
    
while True:
    schedule.run_pending()
    time.sleep(1)
```

Thanks,
@rudSarkar

title: removed a pitfall where a class field was being defined outside the init
body:
**The problem**
There was a class field being defined outside the class \_\_init\_\_
It might be problematic in some scenarios where the code tries to access the field before it is created. It also could hinder the understanding of the code due to the fact the class field definitions are scattered on the source instead of centralized into a single place.

This pitfall was detected automatically via Pylint, which triggered the warning code **W0201** which is described [here](https://vald-phoenix.github.io/pylint-errors/plerr/errors/classes/W0201.html)

**The solution**
Refactored the code to create the field on the \_\_init\_\_

title: Monthly periodicity
body:
Developed monthly periodicity functionality.

Monthly periodicity always need to have defined 'at("DD-HH:MM:SS")' or 'at("DD-HH:MM")', where "DD" is the day of the month it should run.
If "DD"=31 the periodic job will run the last day on the month.

Other exceptions related to end of month dates or February special case are controlled, at least as far as I've been able to check.

title: Feature: Allow multiple times in `every().unit.at()`
body:
This pull request changes the syntax from 
```
schedule.every().minute.at(":00").do(lambda: 0)
schedule.every().minute.at(":05").do(lambda: 0)
schedule.every().minute.at(":10").do(lambda: 0)
```
to
```
schedule.every().minute.at(":00", ":05", ":10").do(lambda: 0)
```
or
```
run_times = (":00", ":05", ":10")
schedule.every().minute.at(*run_times).do(lambda: 0)
```
Current usage should remain unchanged
Resolves https://github.com/dbader/schedule/issues/269
